A bushel is a unit of measurement used mainly to measure quantities of dry goods — things like grain, fruits, and vegetables. Think of it the way you think of a "dozen" (which always means 12 of something) or a "pound" (a unit of weight) — a bushel is simply a well-defined, agreed-upon amount.

Historically, a bushel measured volume — how much space something takes up, the same way a gallon measures how much liquid fits in a container. One US bushel equals approximately 35.24 liters. To picture that: it's roughly the size of a large bucket, or about 9 US gallons. In the UK, the Imperial bushel is slightly larger, at about 36.37 liters.

Within the traditional system of dry measurement, a bushel sits in a clear hierarchy. It equals 4 pecks, or 8 dry gallons, or 32 dry quarts. A peck, if you're wondering, is simply one-quarter of a bushel.
As a Unit of Weight (in modern agriculture and trade)

Here is where it gets more interesting. In modern farming and commodity trading — where enormous quantities of grain like wheat, corn, and soybeans are bought and sold — a bushel is not treated as a volume. Instead, it's used as a unit of weight, and that weight depends on which crop is being measured.

This is because different grains pack differently. A bucket filled with oats will weigh much less than the same bucket filled with wheat, because oat grains are lighter and less dense. So to make trade fair and consistent, specific weights were assigned to each crop. Wheat and soybeans are defined as 60 pounds per bushel. Corn is 56 pounds per bushel. Oats are only 32 pounds per bushel (they're much lighter and fluffier). Barley is 48 pounds per bushel.

So when a farmer says "I harvested 200 bushels of wheat," what they really mean is they harvested 200 × 60 = 12,000 pounds of wheat. And when financial markets trade grain contracts (agreements to buy or sell crops at a future date), they quote prices in dollars per bushel using these exact weight-based definitions.

A bushel is also the name of a physical container — specifically, a large round basket or box designed to hold exactly one bushel of produce. You've likely seen or heard of a "bushel basket" — the wide, open-topped, wicker-style baskets that farmers and market vendors use to carry and display apples, potatoes, tomatoes, and other fruits or vegetables. The container and the measurement share the same name.

Beyond precise measurement, a bushel is used in everyday, informal speech to mean simply a large amount of something. When someone says, "I have a bushel of work to finish," they don't mean anything literal — they just mean they have a lot of work. This is a natural extension of the word: since a bushel is already a sizeable quantity, people began using it loosely to express abundance. This informal sense appears in casual conversation, children's songs, and literature.
Common Expressions That Use This Word

Two idioms involving bushel appear frequently enough that you should know them.

"A bushel and a peck" — A peck is one-fourth of a bushel. So "a bushel and a peck" is a playful expression meaning an overflowing, extra-generous amount. It is used most warmly to express love or affection — you might have heard it in old songs or nursery rhymes: "I love you, a bushel and a peck." It simply means: a whole lot, and then some more on top.

"Hide your light under a bushel" — This idiom comes from the Bible (Matthew 5:15). Imagine lighting a candle, then placing a bushel basket upside down over it — all the light would be trapped and hidden. The expression means to conceal your talents, abilities, or strengths instead of letting them shine. If someone tells you "Don't hide your light under a bushel," they're encouraging you to share your gifts with the world rather than being unnecessarily modest about what you're capable of.
Where You'll Actually Encounter This Word

In agriculture, farmers measure crop yields in bushels per acre. A corn farmer might say, "My field averaged 180 bushels per acre this year." This is how farming productivity is commonly discussed.

In commodity markets and financial news, prices for staple crops like wheat, corn, and soybeans are quoted globally in dollars per bushel. You'll regularly see headlines like "Wheat prices climbed to $6.50 per bushel" in business and agriculture news.

At farm stands and produce markets, goods like apples, peaches, or tomatoes are sometimes still sold by the bushel or half-bushel.

In casual speech and literature, you'll encounter the informal sense — a bushel of laughs, a bushel of trouble, and the tender, affectionate "a bushel and a peck."

A bushel has three layers of meaning: a precise unit of dry volume (historically), a weight-based unit that varies by crop (in modern trade), and a container that holds that amount. On top of these literal meanings, it doubles as an informal expression for "a large amount" and lives on in two well-known idioms. Knowing all three layers means you'll understand this word in every context where you're likely to encounter it.
